JSON: Name: linguistic_domination_pipeline Title: Mixed-methods empirical and experimental analysis of horizontal linguistic domination in multilingual mixed-settlement communities Short Hypothesis: In multilingual mixed-settlement interactions, increased structural markedness of a privileged language causally increases uncontrolled interference by privileged-language speakers (measured as requests-to-switch and imposition of language use), which in turn reduces the probability that vulnerable-language speakers will use their language in subsequent interactions. Related Work: Sociolinguistic research has documented code-switching, diglossia, language ideologies, and how social norms shape individual linguistic choices, often treating linguistic choices as outcomes of internalized social structures. Political-philosophical work on linguistic justice has focused largely on institutional and territorial solutions and proposed parity-of-esteem principles and micro-mechanisms (probability-driven learning, maxi-min use) to explain asymmetric language behaviour. Republican theories of domination provide a conceptual frame for uncontrolled interference but have not been operationalized for interpersonal linguistic contexts. Limitations in the prior literature include: emphasis on either macro-institutional policy or purely descriptive sociolinguistics without causal testing; lack of operational definitions and quantitative measures for uncontrolled interference and markedness; ambiguous mapping from normative concepts (domination, non-domination) to measurable interactional outcomes; and scarce experimental or mixed-methods designs that test causal pathways between social status of languages, agent behaviour, and individual language use. Abstract: This project operationalizes the republican concept of horizontal linguistic domination and tests whether structural markedness of a privileged language produces uncontrolled interference in interpersonal interactions that suppresses vulnerable-language use. We combine observational corpora of multilingual neighborhood and community interactions, randomized vignette surveys, and controlled dyadic interaction experiments to measure requests-to-switch, imposition events, and subsequent language choices. The main contribution is a reproducible empirical pipeline that (1) defines measurable indicators for uncontrolled linguistic interference and markedness; (2) quantifies causal pathways from markedness through interference to reduced vulnerable-language use; and (3) compares these mechanisms against competing explanations derived from existing sociolinguistic models. Expected outcomes include validated operational metrics for linguistic domination, estimates of effect sizes for markedness and discretionary power, and an evidence base to inform normative debate and policy interventions on interpersonal linguistic injustice. Experiments: Datasets: (A) Field interaction corpus: audio/video recordings and transcripts of n=200 community meetings and public interactions across four multilingual mixed-settlement sites (e.g., Welsh/English; Valencian/Spanish; Basque/Spanish; Quebec French/English) yielding ~2,000 annotated interactional episodes. Annotation schema: utterance-level language label, switch_request flag, imposition_flag (explicit demand), speaker demographics, audible sanctions, exit events, and time stamps. (B) Vignette survey: n=1,200 respondents stratified by language group and site; randomized manipulation of speaker status (privileged vs. vulnerable), presence/absence of explicit request-to-switch, and contextual cost level. Outcomes: reported intended language use, perceived domination index (Likert items), and willingness-to-exit. (C) Lab dyadic experiment: n=240 dyads (balanced privileged/vulnerable composition) in controlled tasks where privileged-status cues and demographic majority proportion are experimentally varied; recordings annotated as in (A). Baselines: (1) frequency-only model predicting vulnerable-language use from prior usage rates; (2) sociolinguistic micro-mechanism model operationalizing probability-driven learning and maxi-min use (predictors: estimated expected audience distribution and minimal competence); (3) demographic-only logistic model. Metrics: switch_request_rate (requests per interaction), vulnerable_language_usage_probability (binary per episode), time_to_switch (seconds), perceived_domination_index (standardized score), exit_rate, effect-size (odds ratios), AIC/BIC and cross-validated pseudo-R^2. Statistical setup: mixed-effects logistic regression with random intercepts for speaker and meeting/site; mediation analysis testing markedness -> switch_request_rate -> vulnerable_language_usage_probability; causal identification uses randomized vignette and dyadic manipulations as instruments; pre-registered sample sizes and power analysis targeting 80% power to detect OR=1.5 for markedness effect at alpha=0.05. Ablations/comparisons: remove markedness predictor to quantify variance explained; compare models with and without demographic and ideology covariates; ablate discretionary-condition proxy (demographic majority proportion) to assess its independent contribution. Evaluation: report point estimates, 95% CIs, p-values, and cross-validated predictive performance. Risk Factors and Limitations: Observational confounding: field data are vulnerable to unobserved confounders (e.g., pre-existing interpersonal relationships) that bias causal inference. Measurement validity: operationalizing 'markedness' and 'uncontrolled interference' relies on annotation schemes and subjective coding that may introduce measurement error and inter-annotator variability. Social desirability and Hawthorne effects: recording interactions or survey vignettes may alter participant behaviour. Generalizability limits: results from selected mixed-settlement sites may not transfer to other linguistic ecologies or to immigrant-majority contexts. Sample size and power constraints: rare imposition events may limit statistical power for mediation analyses. Ethical/legal constraints: recording real-world interactions requires consent and may reduce available sample variety. Scalability and compute: manual annotation of multi-site audiovisual corpora is resource-intensive. Causality limits: despite experimental components, inferring long-term structural domination from short-term interactional manipulations remains limited. Bias in self-reports: perceived-domination indices may reflect individual sensitivity rather than objective interference. Finally, cultural and contextual heterogeneity may require site-specific model adjustments, reducing comparability across locations.
